title: Thangka painting
hookLine: painted scrolls made by exact rules, used in meditation

lines: ROLLED UP, CARRIED ON A HORSE.
cards: A painter sits on a cushion with a stretched piece of cotton propped in front of her. She hasn't drawn a single face yet.
With a ruler and a fine charcoal line, she is drawing a grid: a center line, cross lines, careful measured marks, like a builder laying out a house.

Only when the grid is right does the figure begin: the head here, the heart there, the hands exactly so many units from the center. It will take a long time. The finished painting can be rolled up and carried on a horse.

teach.h: A SCROLL THAT ROLLS AND TRAVELS.
teach.b: A thangka is a Tibetan painted scroll, usually on cotton, framed in silk brocade and fitted with a rod so it can be rolled up.
It could travel with a teacher or a nomad family and be hung wherever the practice happened that day. Some monasteries keep giant thangkas that are unrolled across a hillside on festival days.
Thangka painters learn measurement systems handed down in texts and from master to student.
Each kind of figure has its proportions, a peaceful buddha one set, a wrathful protector another, and a painter isn't free to stretch a face or shrink a hand for effect.
The rules carry the teaching, so a figure painted today matches the figure described long ago.
The colors are traditionally ground from minerals and plants, sometimes with gold, and painters train for years under a teacher.
Tradition says the eyes are often painted last; then a lama consecrates the painting, and it is understood to be more than a picture: a support for the presence of what it shows.
And a thangka is made to be looked at in meditation.

A practitioner gazes at the figure, the hands, the colors, the ornaments, then closes the eyes and builds it again in the mind. Here the exact rules matter most. A face drawn by whim would be a different face each time.
A face painted by rule can be held steady, by many people, across generations.

how: Tibetan Buddhists hang thangkas in homes, temples and retreat rooms; trained painters make them to set proportions, a lama consecrates them, and practitioners gaze at them to support visualization in meditation.

games.q: you're a young thangka painter. you think the buddha would look more striking with longer arms. what do you do?
o: paint the longer arms; art is self-expression.
follow the proportions handed down for that figure.
games.why: the painter follows the rules: a figure painted by rule can be held steady in meditation by many people across generations.

practice: Let your eyes rest on one painting, a thangka found online, a print on your wall, a photo you love, taking in the whole first, then going slowly detail by detail: a hand, a color, a small thing in a corner you never noticed.
When you feel you've really seen it, close your eyes and see it again as clearly as you can. Then open them, and look at what you missed.
